front.title: Context Manifests for the CIRIS Agent Trace: Prompt Context Provenance for AI Agent Decision Traces
front.workgroup: Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust

abstract.t: An AI agent that acts on a person's behalf makes each decision through several calls to language models: one stage drafts an action, others evaluate it, and others may veto it. What each call was given decides what it can judge. A record of the action alone cannot show whether a judging stage lacked a rule the drafting stage had, whether untrusted text reached a stage designed never to see it, or whether a stage was prompted in a language other than the one the person used.

This document specifies a per-call context manifest. It describes every contiguous piece of text placed into a model call (a segment) by what it is, where it came from, how far it can be trusted, which authority stands behind it, how long it lives, and which language it is in. It specifies a closed-vocabulary context policy that says which stage may and must receive which kinds of segment, ablation stubs that stand in for text withheld from a stage, and the checks a verifier runs against the manifest and against the bytes actually sent. It states the safety properties of the policy as invariants checked by a model checker. The context manifest is the context_manifest member of the LLM_CALL event of the CIRIS agent trace, carried in a CEG trace row; it can also be the payload of any SCITT signed statement.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Several Internet-Drafts record what an AI agent did: the tool it called, the authorization it held, the decision it reached, and a digest of the model input (). They answer "what was done, by whom, under whose authority". They do not answer a question that comes before it: what was each model call actually given, and was it supposed to be given that?

The question matters because an agent's decision is not one model call. In the agent this document was developed against, a decision passes through up to fourteen call sites in four roles: a drafter that proposes an action, second passes that fill in a chosen verb, evaluators that score the situation, and judges (consciences) that may veto the draft (). Some judges are deliberately denied the untrusted text the drafter saw, so that a persuasive request cannot argue a judge out of its veto. This is input ablation.
Measurement of that agent, before the mechanism in this document existed, found failures that no action record could show ():

list.t: A rule a Wise Authority (the agent's human overseer) had stated reached the drafter, but almost never the two ablated judges. The judges then vetoed compliant replies as "invented policy".
The reason for a veto never reached the stage asked to revise the draft (0 of 162 retries).
Raw user text reached the ablated judges inside a system-built record of earlier actions, in about a third of first-pass calls. The ablation leaked.
A user's self-chosen display name was laid out where a verified identity belonged.

section.t: All four were found by pattern-matching 42,998 prompts after the fact. This document makes the same facts a signed record of every call.

section.name: What This Document Adds
section.t: Five properties distinguish this profile from the agent trace drafts surveyed in . As far as the author has found, none of them is specified elsewhere for agent traces.

list.t: Provenance of each piece of context. Each segment carries its kind, provenance, source, trust level and lifecycle, and the authentication, authorization and accounting records that make it binding (). Trust propagates: a segment is no more trusted than any segment whose bytes it contains.

Withholding with a record. A stage may be given a stub in place of a segment: closed-vocabulary properties of the withheld text, never its bytes (). The manifest records what was withheld and a digest of it, and a verifier checks that the withheld bytes do not appear elsewhere in the call.
Language as evidence. Each segment records the locale its bytes were rendered in and how that is known, and the manifest lists the segments that fell back to another language ().
Machine-checked policy. The context policy is compiled from a closed vocabulary. The same source generates the runtime guard and a TLA+ specification whose invariants a model checker verifies ().
Declared against observed. Each segment records its span and a digest of its bytes in the message actually sent, so a verifier can check that the manifest describes the call and not an intention ().

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document specifies the manifest, the policy vocabulary, the stub, and the checks. It does not specify how an agent decides, what any stage concludes, or how a tool call is authorized: the manifest records what models were given, not whether they were right. It defines no trace envelope, signature, receipt or transparency mechanism: the trace and its levels are , the signed row and admission are , and transparency is .
"Context manifest" is used throughout, never "manifest" alone. It is unrelated to the trace_manifest:v1 object of , which carries a trace too large to inline.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dd.t: One request to a language model.
A named call site in the agent's decision procedure. Every call belongs to exactly one stage.
What a stage does: drafter, second_pass, evaluator or judge ().
A stage that by policy receives no untrusted text.
One contiguous run of text placed into a call, described as in .
The component that builds a call's messages from segments, enforces the policy, and emits the manifest. An implementation conforming to this document has exactly one assembler path for every call.
The table that says, for each stage and each kind of segment, whether the stage must, may or must not receive it, and in which form ().
The per-call record specified in . Where this document says "manifest" it means a context manifest.
The closed-vocabulary description sent in place of a withheld segment ().
A human party whose signed grants make rules binding on the agent. The term is that of ; any deployment's equivalent overseer fills the same role here.

section.name: The Decision Model
section.t: A decision is the work an agent does on one thought: a unit of reasoning within a task. The stages of the model are:

texttable.title: Stages and their roles
texttable.c: drafter
aspdma (action selection)
second_pass
tsaspdma, dsaspdma, fsaspdma, msaspdma, rsaspdma (one per verb: tool, defer, forget, memorize, recall)
evaluator
csdma (common sense), dsdma (domain), pdma (principles), idma (intuition)
judge
coherence, epistemic, entropy, optveto (optimization veto)

section.t: Evaluators run first and their results reach the drafter. The drafter proposes an action; a second pass completes it for its verb. Every judge then reviews the draft. A veto sends the thought back to the drafter with typed feedback (a retry), up to a depth limit. A draft that survives review is executed.

A deployment MAY name different stages. This profile requires only that each stage has a stable name, one role, and an entry in the policy, and that the set of ablated stages is declared in the policy.

In the reference implementation the ablated stages are entropy and optveto. They judge the draft against the agent's own commitments and against signed rules, but never see the request that prompted it.

section.name: Segment Taxonomy
section.t: A segment is described on six independent axes. The kind says what the text is; provenance, source, trust and lifecycle say where it came from and what it is worth; locale says what language it is in. Keeping the axes separate is deliberate: the earlier measurement mixed them, and the mixing is how leaks hid.

section.name: Kind

texttable.title: Segment kinds
texttable.c: the stage's own prompt: role, task, output contract
output-schema text a provider library appends to the call
the agent's governing ethical text
the agent's configured identity
one approved, signed change to the agent's identity
a behavioural rule in force for this request, with its provenance
a Wise Authority's guidance from a resolved deferral
the message being answered
earlier messages in the conversation
the verified sender: subject, role, and what verified them
the sender's self-chosen name
the factual record of actions already taken in the task
the proposed action under review
an evaluator's result passed downstream
a typed veto passed to a retry
a tool's result
where the stage sits and what it cannot see

section.t: sender_identity and display_name are separate kinds so that no layout can present a name as an identity. A sender_identity segment carries no text of its own: the assembler renders it from its authentication carrier ().

section.name: Provenance
section.t: Provenance applies to rule segments only, and is REQUIRED on them.

texttable.title: Rule provenance
texttable.c: stated by a user in conversation
untrusted
stated by a Wise Authority in conversation, unsigned
untrusted
from a resolved deferral whose grant signature verified
verified
from a landed, signed identity amendment
verified

section.t: A rule stated in conversation is advisory, whoever states it. It remains part of the request or history segment it was said in. In the reference policy no stage lists rule.user_chat or rule.wa_chat, so no such segment is ever produced; the values exist so that a policy that admitted one would be expressible and checkable.

section.name: Source
section.t: Which component produced the bytes: user_input, adapter_metadata, auth_context, signed_row, agent_profile, engine, llm_output, tool_output or provider_lib. A kind MAY be restricted by the policy to one source.

section.name: Trust
section.t: Trust has three ordered levels: untrusted < verified < system.

list.t: untrusted: user-controlled or model-generated text.
verified: established by the system against a credential or a signature.
system: produced by the agent from its own state.

section.t: The policy assigns each kind (and each rule provenance) a trust level. A producer MAY state a lower trust for a segment than the policy's; it MUST NOT state a higher one.

Taint rule. A segment's trust after taint is the minimum of its own trust and the trust after taint of every segment listed in its derived_from. The manifest records trust after taint. An action_record that quotes a user's words is therefore untrusted, whichever component built it. A segment whose trust after taint is below the trust the policy requires for its kind is a tainted violation ().

section.name: Lifecycle
section.t: How long a segment lives: standing, per-task, per-message, per-thought, retry-only or per-call. A per-task or per-thought segment records the task or thought it belongs to; one placed in a call for another task or thought is a cross_scope violation.

section.name: AAA Carriers
section.t: Each segment MAY carry three records. The policy states which are REQUIRED for which kind.

dd.t: The verified subject: subject identifier, role, and the verifier that established them. REQUIRED on sender_identity.

The grant that makes the segment binding: its kind (amendment, deferral or response_attestation), its identifier, the authorizer, whether its signature verified, and when it was granted. REQUIRED on amendment, on rule with provenance signed_guidance or amendment, and on wa_guidance.
The record tying the segment to the audit trail: audit entry, the hash of the signed row its bytes came from, the trace, and for conscience_feedback the veto and discharge identifiers.

section.t: A judge that is asked whether a rule binds reads the rule's authz carrier, attested by the system, not prose claiming authority.

section.name: Locale
section.t: Each segment records locale, a language tag , and locale_basis:

dd.t: The producer stated the locale it actually served, after any fallback. For text read from a localized prompt file, this is the file read, not the file requested.
The assembler rendered the bytes itself (for example, a sender line from its carrier in the call's language, or a stub line).
No component vouches for a locale. User text, model output, and text authored in an agent's configuration are unstated unless their producer states otherwise.

section.t: Two tags have fixed meanings here: mul for text that is deliberately multilingual (a polyglot prompt), and zxx for closed-vocabulary tokens with no linguistic content (a stub line).

The call records language, the locale it was rendered for. A segment is a locale fallback when its basis is declared, its locale is neither mul nor zxx, and its primary language subtag differs from that of the call's language. The manifest lists every fallback segment in locale_fallbacks. A regional variant (pt-BR in a pt call) is not a fallback.

A segment joined from fields served in different locales (for example, a localized paragraph followed by one that fell back to English) records the locale that differs from the call's language, so that the segment is listed as a fallback. A per-field fallback is a fallback: a producer that serves one field of a localized prompt from another language MUST record that field's segment with the language actually served.

The reason this is evidence and not configuration: a judge prompted partly in English while the person wrote in Amharic is a different judge. In the reference implementation this was first found by counting script characters in sent prompts; with this record it is a field of every call.

section.name: The Context Policy
section.t: The policy is a single document. It has five parts:

dd.t: An integer.
The stages that receive no untrusted text.

For each kind: its trust (absent for rule, whose trust comes from provenance), its lifecycle, which carriers are REQUIRED, whether it is rendered with a label, whether it is an accepted residual (), and the one source it may have, if fixed.
The trust of each rule provenance.
For each stage, an ordered list of rows. A row is a kind (or rule.<provenance>), a predicate, and a form. Row order is the stage's rendering order.
The closed set of fields a stub may carry ().

section.name: Predicates
section.t: A row's predicate says when the stage receives the kind. The predicates are a closed set, each evaluated against facts the system establishes from its own state (signed rows, the authentication context), never from the segments being checked:

texttable.title: Policy predicates
texttable.c: always
never
the call is a retry after a veto
signed WA guidance from a resolved deferral applies
a landed identity amendment carries a rule that applies
either of the two above
the rule in force is scoped to a verified identity
an unsigned rule was stated in conversation

section.t: When a predicate holds, the kind is REQUIRED at that stage; a call without it is a missing_required violation. When it does not hold, or the kind has no row, the kind is forbidden. Facts MUST NOT be derived from the segments, or a missing rule could hide itself.

section.name: Form
section.t: A row's form is full (the segment's bytes are sent) or stub (a stub is sent in place of the bytes). A stub row is permitted only at an ablated stage, and only for an untrusted kind.

section.name: Static Checks
section.t: A policy is admissible only if a compiler confirms all of the following before it is deployed. The reference compiler refuses a policy that fails any of them.

list.t: Closed vocabulary. Every kind, provenance, source, trust, lifecycle, predicate, form and stub field is one this document names.
Firewall. At an ablated stage, every untrusted kind is either absent, a stub row, or a declared residual.
Signed rules only. No stage requires a rule whose provenance is untrusted.
No laundering. A kind the policy marks system is admitted only with an empty derived_from at runtime; the assembler enforces this per call.
Identity layout. Any stage that admits display_name admits it only as a labelled kind, never inside sender_identity.
Evidence sufficiency. Wherever a trusted rule can be in force, every judge receives that rule with its authorization carrier.
Coverage. Every declared kind is used by some stage, and every stage is assigned a role.

section.t: The same policy source generates the runtime guard, the TLA+ contract () and the conformance tests, so that code, model and behaviour cannot silently diverge.

section.name: Residuals
section.t: Some untrusted text cannot be withheld from a judge without defeating the judge. The draft under review is the main case: it may quote the request. A policy names such kinds as residuals. A residual is sent in full at an ablated stage, is excluded from the leak check (), and is recorded as untrusted. Residuals are a stated limit of the ablation, not an exception to it.

section.name: Ablation Stubs
section.t: A stub tells an ablated stage that something was withheld, and what kind of thing it was, without its bytes. Without a stub the stage would judge a draft that answers a question it cannot know was asked.
A stub's fields are drawn only from this closed set; a policy's stub_fields selects which are rendered:

texttable.title: Stub fields
texttable.c: the withheld segment's kind
for a rule: its provenance
the withheld segment's source
its trust after taint (always untrusted for a stub)
the author's verified role, or unauthenticated
none, advisory, or signed (only with a verified grant)
this_turn, this_task, standing
the engine's state for it, per kind (below)
engine operations applied: sanitized, truncated, normalized, redacted, coalesced
none, responds_to, quotes; with quote_share 0, <10%, 10-50%, >50%
short (at most 200 characters), medium (at most 1000), long
current or prior_<n>
the first 12 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256 of the withheld bytes

section.t: Dispositions are per kind: a request is open, answered, deferred or refused; a rule is advisory_unsigned, awaiting_signature or refused; a tool output is success or failure; history is prior.
quote_share is the share of the withheld segment's character 8-grams (after whitespace collapsing and case folding) that the draft repeats. It is computed deterministically and never by a model.

Every field value comes from the engine's state or from a deterministic function of the bytes. No field carries text of the withheld segment, and no field is produced by a model. The rendered stub line is assembler-rendered with locale zxx.

section.name: Encoding
section.t: The manifest is a CBOR map with text-string keys, encoded deterministically (Section 4.2 of ) when it is the payload of a signed statement. Following , it contains no floating-point values: every number is an integer. Digests are SHA-256 .

The reference implementation emits the same structure as JSON on its reasoning stream, with digests as lowercase hexadecimal text. A producer that signs a manifest converts each digest to a byte string of 32 octets (6 octets for a stub digest), omits each optional member the JSON form gives as null, and otherwise keeps the structure.

section.name: CDDL
section.t: The manifest is specified in CDDL .

figure.title: The context manifest

dd.t: Unique per call. When the producer has none, it is the first 32 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256 over the stage, task, thought, retry index and messages digest joined by |.
0 on the first pass, n on the n-th retry after a veto.
SHA-256 of the policy document's bytes. A verifier MUST hold the policy with this digest to run the checks of .

fail_closed means a violation aborts the call (used in testing and QA). strip_and_incident means the offending segment is removed, an incident is recorded, and the call proceeds (used in production). A manifest with violations in fail_closed mode never accompanies a sent call.

In rendering order. message_index and [span_start, span_end) locate the segment in the content of the message sent, in Unicode scalar values. sha256 is over the UTF-8 encoding of exactly that span. For a stub segment, the span holds the stub line, stub holds the stub, and withheld_sha256 is over the UTF-8 encoding of the withheld bytes.

A digest of the messages as sent. Form ciris-json-1 is the form the reference implementation's model bus hashes: a JSON array of the message objects in order, each with role and content, members in insertion order, separators ", " and ": ", non-ASCII characters unescaped, encoded as UTF-8. Form jcs is the JSON Canonicalization Scheme over the same array. Absent means ciris-json-1. New implementations SHOULD use jcs and state it.
Set by the component that sent the call: true when the messages it sent hash to messages_sha256. Absent when the manifest was not finalized at the sending component.

Whether text a provider library added to the call (for example, an output schema appended to the last message) was reproduced and recorded as schema_instruction segments. unrecognized_change means the library rewrote the messages in a way the producer could not record; a verifier treats such a call's segment list as incomplete.

section.name: Guard Violations
section.t: The assembler checks every call against the policy before it is sent:

texttable.title: Guard violations
texttable.c: the policy does not admit this kind at this stage in this state
a required kind is absent
trust after taint is below the policy's trust for the kind
a required authn, authz or acct is absent
the kind's fixed source differs
a stated lifecycle differs from the policy's
a per-task or per-thought segment from another task or thought
two segments share an identifier in one call
at an ablated stage, a withheld segment's bytes were found inside another, non-residual segment

section.t: A violation's detail explains it and MUST NOT contain segment text.

The untrusted_bytes check normalizes text by collapsing whitespace and case folding, then looks for windows of 32 characters taken every 16 characters (at most 256 windows) of each withheld segment of at least 20 characters, inside every other segment that is neither a residual nor attested by a verified grant.

section.name: Verifying a Manifest
section.t: A verifier holds the manifest, the policy whose digest the manifest names, and, where available, the messages as sent. It runs these checks and reports each as passed, failed, or not run with the reason.

dd.t: Recompute, from the segment records and the facts the verifier can establish, every violation of except untrusted_bytes. Report any the manifest does not list.

With the messages as sent: recompute messages_sha256, and for each segment the digest of its span. Report any mismatch. This is the check that catches a call that bypassed the assembler, or a manifest that misdescribes its call.
Recompute trust after taint from derived_from and the policy. Report any segment recorded at a higher trust.

At each ablated stage, confirm every untrusted, non-residual segment has form stub; with the messages as sent and the withheld bytes, run the untrusted_bytes search over the text outside residual spans.
Confirm each required carrier is present, and that every authz with signature_verified true resolves to a grant whose signature the verifier can check.

Recompute locale_fallbacks from the segment records and language. A deployment that requires a locale MAY additionally require that no segment of kind stage_instruction or pipeline_position is a fallback.
Report provider_capture values unsupported_mode, unrecognized_change and unavailable: the segment list may not cover the call.

section.t: A verifier that lacks the messages as sent can run V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7. V2 and V4 require the bytes. This separation lets a manifest be published while the prompts, which may hold personal data, are not ().

section.name: Formal Model
section.t: The policy's safety properties are stated as invariants of a TLA+ specification and checked with the TLC model checker. The specification, H3EREContextFlow.tla, models one thought through drafting, judging, retry and execution across six scenarios (no rule; a user's own preference; an unsigned WA rule; signed WA guidance; a signed amendment; an identity-scoped amendment with an impersonation attempt) and a bounded retry depth. Its context inputs are generated: the contract configuration from the policy by the compiler of (ContractPolicy.tla), and the measured configuration from manifests and sent prompts of real runs (ContextData.tla).
The invariants, by name, as checked at :

texttable.title: Invariants of H3EREContextFlow.tla
texttable.c: no ablated judge receives an untrusted kind
when a trusted rule is in force, every judge receives it
under an identity-scoped rule, every judge receives the verified sender
no judge receives a system segment carrying untrusted bytes
WA guidance reaches judges only within its own task
a display name never appears inside the sender line
stubs appear only at ablated stages
an executed action is acceptable for its scenario
the action executed is the action reviewed, or a refusal the tool gate forced
a vetoed action executes only after its veto is discharged
once refused for lack of authority, the action is not later executed
no deferral is forced by the depth limit alone
every deferral carries its package to the WA
every thought reaches a final state

section.t: Results at : the contract configuration satisfies all fourteen invariants. The configuration measured from the reference agent before the mechanism of this document (version 2.22.1) violates ten of them. A variant of the contract that admits one unreviewed change after review violates ReviewIntegrity, VetoContinuity, AuthMonotone and NoWrongExecution; adding the tool gate restores AuthMonotone only. These are model-checking results over a finite abstraction, not proofs about the implementation; the manifest is what connects the two, since the measured configuration is generated from it.

section.name: Placement in the CIRIS Agent Trace
The LLM_CALL Member
section.t: The CIRIS agent trace records each thought as a CompleteTrace: ordered pipeline components, and one LLM_CALL event per provider call, linked to the pipeline event that issued it. The context manifest of a call is the LLM_CALL event's context_manifest member. It is inside the trace's signed canonical bytes, so an aggregator cannot detach it or attach it to another call without invalidating the trace signature.
The trace's disclosure levels apply:

texttable.title: The context manifest at each trace level
texttable.c: omitted (the level carries no prompt digests)
present; each authn.subject_id is the first 16 hexadecimal digits of HMAC-SHA256 over the identifier string under a per-agent secret, with subject_id_form hmac_sha256_16
present; subject_id as verified, with subject_id_form raw (or absent)

section.t: The secret is held by the agent and never disclosed in a trace. User identifiers are often low-entropy (a chat platform's numeric identifier, a short handle), so an unkeyed hash could be reversed by trying candidates and would link one person across every agent's traces. The keyed form is stable within one agent, so a verifier can still tell that two calls answered the same sender, and is not linkable across agents.

At detailed, the LLM_CALL event also carries prompt_hash, which is the manifest's messages_sha256: the two MUST be equal. At full_traces the event carries the prompt itself, so checks V2 and V4 of can run from the trace alone.

section.name: As a CEG Trace Row
section.t: In , an agent's own reasoning trace is a row of the family trace:{form}:{version}; specifies its trace:complete:v1 form. For context manifests the following rules of that form matter:

list.t: The row is signed only by the agent's own key. (Section 3.1.5) assigns the trace family's attest and withdraw uses to the agent signer kind; a node, host or person key MUST NOT sign it. The machine-checkable form is the key-role contract of (manifests/key_roles.json, family trace:{form}:{version}, signer kind agent).

The row names its run: run_kind is in the signed bytes, from the closed set of (production, prod-personal, prod-managed, qa, battery, mock). A mock trace is refused at federation-tier admission outright, with refusal token trace_run_kind_mock: a mock model's output attests nothing about any agent. A node MAY hold its own mock rows locally (for QA and tests).

The manifests of a thought's calls ride in its LLM_CALL events, in call order. The payload is deterministically encoded CBOR with no floating-point values. Any score or confidence elsewhere in the trace is a fixed6 integer, as requires.
The policy document a manifest names by policy_sha256 SHOULD itself be published as a signed row, so that a verifier can obtain it.

section.t: The signed object, its signature, its names and references, and its admission are those of ; this document repeats none of them.

section.name: As a SCITT Signed Statement
section.t: Outside the CIRIS trace, a context manifest MAY be the payload of any SCITT signed statement (a COSE_Sign1 message registered with a transparency service). The checks of are unchanged. Two guarantees of a CEG row are lost:

list.t: The family's door. A CEG node admits a trace row only if its family's static checks pass, including the closed run_kind. A generic transparency service admits a statement without inspecting its payload, so a mock or malformed manifest can be registered.

The key-role check. A CEG node refuses a trace row signed by any key but the agent's own. Outside CEG, nothing binds the signer of a manifest to the agent whose calls it describes; a verifier MUST establish that binding by other means before relying on it.

section.name: Relationship to Other Work
section.t: Several individual Internet-Drafts record agent actions in SCITT-style statements. Measured against the five properties of the Introduction:

list.t: digests the request and response octets at each model call, which this document's messages_sha256 and span digests also provide. It records digests of the system prompt and skills, but not who supplied each piece of context or at what trust, and its digest is taken before any content is withheld; it has no notion of a stage denied some context.
attests a taint level for a context window per tool call, and refuses a call rather than withholding content. This document's taint rule is per segment and its stubs record withholding.

, , and record actions, decisions, delegation and input hashes, and some redact the stored record. Redacting a record after the fact is different from withholding text from a model before the call, which is what a stub records.
attributes each message of an agent conversation to a party.
The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions define spans for model calls and can capture input messages, but carry no provenance, trust or signature.

describes an architecture for auditing agent delegation and interactions across domains, and the attestation and registry evidence for delegation traceability. specifies verifiable records of agent conversations. These address what passed between parties; this document addresses what each model call inside one party was given.

section.t: None of these, as far as the author has found, records the locale of model input or states its properties as model-checked invariants. This document is complementary to all of them: an action record can reference the manifests of the calls behind the action.

section.name: Relationship to the AUDIT Charter
section.t: The proposed AUDIT working group would define interoperable audit records for agents and delegated systems, verifiable by a party that trusts neither the agent nor its operator. The table below maps each signal the draft charter names to where a deployment of with this profile carries it.

texttable.title: AUDIT draft-charter signals and where they are carried
texttable.c: Attribution to a user, agent instance or delegation context
the trace row is signed by the agent's own key; the authn carrier names the verified sender; delegation is a CEG delegates_to row
Delegation chains
delegates_to rows and their references ()
Authorization as a time-evolving state
authz carriers with grant identifier, authorizer, signature status and grant time; the grant's own rows, replaced and withdrawn by later rows; the policy predicates evaluated per call
Identity transitions
key records and identity amendments as signed rows; amendment segments with their grants
User intent declarations
the request segment (its digest, and its stub where withheld)
Agent and tool interactions, exchanged data
tool_output, dma_output and draft segments with span digests; messages_sha256 per call
Invoked or declined actions, and outcomes
the trace's terminal result (completed, refused, deferred); typed vetoes in conscience_feedback
Execution context and structure as it emerges
one manifest per call, in call order, with stage, role, retry index and thought kind
Verifiable without trusting agent or operator
signed rows with transparency receipts; check V2 against bytes captured by a party the agent does not control ()
Privacy and selective disclosure without disclosing prompts
manifests carry identifiers, digests and closed-vocabulary values, never text; CEG members can be blinded (selective disclosure); V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7 run without the prompts

section.t: This profile also carries signals the draft charter does not ask for: per-segment provenance and trust with taint, withholding with a record, locale, and machine-checked policy invariants.
Two charter items are not covered here, and are not claimed:

list.t: Cross-domain correlation in protocols. CEG rows reference one another by name, and a manifest names its task and thought, but this document defines no identifier propagated across other parties' protocols (HTTP headers, token claims) to link one interaction across administrative domains. That is the charter's third deliverable, and the identifier is expected from the agentproto working group.

Evidence from parties other than the agent. A trace row is the agent's own account. Correlating it with records made by tools, services and other agents in other domains, where no single party has the whole picture, needs those parties' records; this profile is one of them, not the collection.

section.t: The draft charter places the auditing of "the underlying AI model, training data, or inference mechanisms" out of scope while allowing interactions with the model. A manifest describes what each model call was given and under which policy, not how the model computes; it is a record of an interaction with the model, in the charter's terms.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: Note to the RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication, together with the reference to .
This section records the status of known implementations at the time of writing, as described in . Listing an implementation here does not imply endorsement.

dd.t: , CIRIS L3C, AGPL-3.0. The assembler, the policy file ciris_engine/data/context_policy.yaml, the runtime guard, ablation stubs and the per-call manifest are on the main branch at commit 59b7e5d (pull request 1367). The locale record of is in pull request 1368, not yet merged at the time of writing. The implementation emits each manifest as JSON, with hexadecimal digests and the ciris-json-1 messages form, on the llm_call event of its reasoning stream. Its signed traces carry each call's messages_sha256 (as prompt_hash); adding context_manifest to the signed LLM_CALL event, with keyed subject pseudonyms at detailed (), is in progress and not yet in a released trace schema. It does not emit messages_digest_form. The reference policy compiler and the TLA+ specification are in formal/h3ere_ctxflow/ of the same repository.

CIRIS L3C. A context-map harness that drives the agent through the six scenarios with a deterministic mock model and checks every call's manifest against the policy and against the bytes sent (checks V1, V2, V4, and a script-based locale check that predates V6). On the merged implementation it found the Amharic-locale gap that now records directly.

section.t: No second, independent implementation exists.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: What the manifest proves. A manifest signed by the agent's key is the agent's own account of its calls. Check V2 against independently captured bytes (for example, at a model gateway the agent does not control) is what turns that account into evidence. Without it, a compromised agent can emit a consistent but false manifest.

Ablation is a stated limit, not a guarantee. Residuals are untrusted text sent to ablated stages by design. The leak check is a substring search over normalized text: paraphrase, translation or encoding defeats it. It detects copying, not influence.

Stubs leak properties. A stub reveals the kind, size bucket, author role and disposition of withheld text, and its quote share reveals how much of it the draft repeats. The field set is closed so that what leaks is known.

Facts versus segments. Policy predicates are evaluated against facts from trusted state. An implementation that derived them from the segments could let a missing rule hide itself, or let a forged segment make itself required.
Provider libraries. A library that rewrites messages after the assembler can add text the policy never admitted. The provider_capture field makes that visible; it cannot prevent it.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: A manifest contains identifiers, digests and closed-vocabulary values, never segment text; violation details never contain segment text. It does contain subject identifiers in authn carriers, which are personal data where the subject is a person. In the CIRIS trace they are disclosed as verified only at full_traces; at detailed they are keyed pseudonyms (), and at generic no context manifest is sent.

Digests of short, guessable text can be inverted by trying candidates. withheld_sha256 and the stub digest of a short request (a size of short is at most 200 characters) are open to this. A deployment that publishes manifests SHOULD replace these with keyed digests whose key is held with the prompts, or omit them, and record which it did; the reference implementation uses unkeyed SHA-256 and is affected.
Publishing manifests while withholding prompts is the intended use: V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7 run on the manifest alone.

front.title: Tags for Identifying Languages

abstract.t: This document describes the structure, content, construction, and semantics of language tags for use in cases where it is desirable to indicate the language used in an information object. It also describes how to register values for use in language tags and the creation of user-defined extensions for private interchange. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

front.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)

abstract.t: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

The CIRIS Agent Reasoning Trace
Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)

abstract.t: Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: Agent Execution Evidence: A SCITT Profile for Verifiable Records of AI Agent Runs

abstract.t: AI agents act through calls to models, tools and other agents. Identity work establishes who an agent is and what it may do, but leaves execution-evidence formats and assurance criteria out of scope. This document profiles the Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT) architecture for Signed Statements that bind an agent's registered identity, declared capabilities, risk-based assessment and supervised operational status to a hash- chained record of every call the agent makes. It also defines admission records produced where a call is received, and the linking of records for requests that pass between agents of different operators. It specifies Registration Policy, offline verification and Bundle requirements. It does not define an accreditation scheme, a universal risk classification, an identifier scheme or a policy language.

front.title: Cryptographic Separation of Untrusted Data-Plane Context from Control-Plane Tool Invocations in Autonomous AI Agents

abstract.t: Autonomous AI agents operating over Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) transports routinely ingest untrusted external data (emails, web documents, retrieved RAG chunks) into the same inference context that authorizes privileged control-plane tool calls. Existing workload identity and token standards (OAuth 2.1, GNAP, WIMSE Wit/Wpt tokens) bind client identity and authorization scope, but fail to cryptographically bind the provenance taint of the data-plane context that induced the tool invocation, leaving systems vulnerable to indirect prompt-injection confused-deputy attacks. This document specifies a deterministic COSE_Sign1 and JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS, RFC 8785) wire profile that attaches a cryptographic Context Taint Attestation (CTA) header to every control-plane tool invocation, forcing relying parties to fail closed when an untrusted or mixed data-plane context attempts to trigger a state-mutating action without an independent out-of-band human or policy approval receipt.

front.title: Agent Audit Trail: A Standard Logging Format for Autonomous AI Systems

abstract.t:
This document specifies a standard logging format for autonomous AI agent systems. The Agent Audit Trail (AAT) defines a JSON-based record structure with mandatory fields for agent identity, the authorizing principal, action classification, outcome tracking, and trust level reporting. Records are linked via tamper-evident hash chaining using SHA-256 per RFC 8785, with optional ECDSA signatures for non-repudiation.
The format addresses requirements from the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), which mandates automatic recording of events for high-risk AI systems, whose application dates were staged into 2027-2028 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. It also maps informatively to SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, ISO/IEC 42001, the draft ISO/IEC 24970 and prEN 18229-1 logging standards, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 logging requirements.
The design is transport-agnostic and supports export to JSONL, Syslog (RFC 5424), and CSV while preserving chain integrity. Privacy is addressed through input/output hashing, content fingerprinting, and tombstone-based deletion compatible with GDPR Article 17.
The -01 revision added pre-execution recording requirements, recording independence, deny reason codes, replay protection, external timestamp anchoring, and content fingerprinting based on feedback from independent implementers.
The -02 revision added a Decision Reproducibility section (Section 13) that distinguishes record reproducibility, available for any model, from decision reproducibility, available only for open-weight models executed at temperature zero in an attested environment, and defines the associated record fields.
The -03 revision added the Attestation Closure requirement (Section 13.6): the digests recorded for decision reproducibility MUST cover the complete computational closure of the inference function -- model weights, tokenizer, chat template, inference engine build, decoding configuration, and numeric environment -- together with new record fields (tokenizer_digest, chat_template_digest, engine_build_digest) and a minimal-change threat analysis (Section 13.7) showing that any component left outside the attested set is a forgery channel.
The -04 revision added algorithm agility for post-quantum signatures (ML-DSA-65, FIPS 204) alongside ECDSA P-256; a key identifier (signer_kid, RFC 7638) that resolves which principal signed an independently recorded record; a trust-level assignment integrity requirement (Section 5.3) so that downgrading a consequential action is an attributable event rather than silent suppression; and OPTIONAL Merkle batch anchoring (Section 6.4) using the RFC 6962 construction for compact inclusion proofs at high throughput. All -04 additions are OPTIONAL to produce, and -04 verifiers stay backward compatible with -03: a -04 verifier accepts -03 records, and the new signing metadata is required only in records that carry a signature.
This revision (-07) adds a mandatory "principal" field (Section 3.1) that binds each record to the party on whose authority the agent acted; a Relationship to Other Work section (Section 1.3) relating AAT to the WIMSE agent audit record and authorization-evidence drafts and to SCITT (RFC 9943); and corrections to the EU AI Act Article 12 and Article 19 citations in the regulatory mapping (Section 11.1 and Appendix B). Records produced under -06 and earlier predate the "principal" field; verifiers processing mixed-revision archives SHOULD treat its absence as "principal not recorded" rather than a validation failure.
The -10 revision strengthens recording independence (Section 5.2) from SHOULD to MUST at trust level L2 and above, and requires the "authority_ref" of the "principal" field (Section 3.1) to be non-null and to reference an authorization artifact verifiable independently of the agent at L2 and above, in response to independent review. Above L2, both the recorder and the authorizing artifact are therefore independent of the agent.

front.title: AI Agent Execution Profile of SCITT

abstract.t: This document defines a SCITT (Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust) profile for creating independently verifiable, tamper- evident records of autonomous AI agent actions. The profile defines the AgentInteractionRecord (AIR) as the COSE_Sign1 signed statement payload for material agent actions; maps SCITT roles to the agent execution context, with the Agent Operator as Issuer and an independent Evidence Custodian as Transparency Service; specifies Registration Policy requirements including hash chain integrity, temporal ordering, and sequence completeness; defines a redaction receipt mechanism for privacy-preserving evidence custody; and provides compliance mappings to EU AI Act Articles 12 and 19, DORA, NIST AI RMF, MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines, PCI DSS, and MiFID II.

front.title: An Agent Action Capsule Profile for SCITT

abstract.t: This document defines a SCITT statement profile for recording what an AI agent did: the Agent Action Capsule. A Capsule is a digest- committed record of one agent action carrying its verdict-level disposition (executed, blocked, denied, errored, timed out), the deterministic constraints that were evaluated, the effect that was committed together with a confirmed-effect binding that distinguishes a dispatched attempt from an observed result, and an honest human-in- the-loop flag. Capsules are identified independently of signing and MAY be authenticated by one or more COSE_Sign1 Producer Envelopes. Its Capsule ID can separately be made transparent by registration in a SCITT Transparency Service [I-D.ietf-scitt-scrapi]. A Capsule is recorded on every verdict, including refusals: a blocked or denied Capsule is the auditor-grade evidence that a gate worked.

front.title: An AI Agent Extension for Virtualized Conversations (vCon)

abstract.t: AI agents that use large language models increasingly perform consequential tasks on behalf of humans and other AI agents. Demonstrating that recorded AI agent behavior truthfully represents actual behavior is essential for accountability, compliance, and human oversight. To achieve that goal, this document defines an extension to the Virtualized Conversation (vCon) object format, allowing a vCon to capture a conversation between a human and an AI agent, or between AI Agents. The vCon core format can already capture the back and forth messages (including text and voice) sent by AI agents, but additional extensions are required to fully reproduce the AI agent trajectory, such as agent metadata, message exchanges, tool invocations, reasoning traces, system events, file attribution, etc. This document defines those extensions in both descriptive language and formal CDDL definitions. This draft is a replacement for the former Verifiable Agent Conversation Records specification, which was a standalone format and not an extension of vCon.

front.title: An Audit Record Format for AI Agent Authorization Decisions

abstract.t: This document defines a record format for AI agent authorization decisions and the effects that followed them. The format is one in- toto predicate type, signed inside a DSSE envelope. A record carries the decision and the observed effect with a derived agreement between them, whether the decision point could evaluate the request and how fresh each input it relied on was, and a canonicalization contract under which a party that trusts neither the agent nor its operator recomputes the record's consistency from its bytes. The document also defines what a party that retains a record keeps beside it, so that the record can later be dated from anchors that party does not control. The format carries the seven minimum audit fields of the WIMSE AI Identity Management System framework, and it is offered as a data model for the audit records the proposed AUDIT working group would specify. It defines no policy.

front.title: An Architecture for Auditing Agent Delegation and Interactions

abstract.t: This document describes an architecture for auditing of agent-driven interactions on the Internet. Autonomous and semi-autonomous software agents, including those based on artificial intelligence, increasingly act on behalf of users, organizations, and services. Existing auditing mechanisms often capture isolated system events but do not consistently represent delegation relationships, user intent, or evolving authorization. In agent-driven systems, auditability requires linking intent, delegation, authorization, and execution. The proposed architecture enables this through distributed audit record generation, propagation of audit context, optional attestation, and additional logging for transparency.

front.title: Verifiable Agent Conversation Records

abstract.t: Autonomous agents based on large language models increasingly perform consequential tasks on behalf of humans and other agents. Demonstrating that recorded agent behavior truthfully represents actual behavior is essential for accountability, compliance, and human oversight. This document defines a data format for verifiable agent conversation records using CDDL, with representations in both JSON and CBOR. The format captures session metadata, message exchanges, tool invocations, reasoning traces, and system events in a structured, extensible CDDL definition for verifiable agent conversation records. COSE is used as the signing method to allow for native interoperability in SCITT Transparency Services and the CDDL definition allows for seemless integration in Evidence as specified in RFC 9334. The specification supports cross-vendor interoperability by defining a common representation that accommodates translation from multiple existing agent implementations with distinct data structure layouts that are typically represented in JSON.

front.title: Delegation and Interaction Traceability for AI Agents: An Attestation and Registry Evidence Model

abstract.t:
AI agents increasingly act through chains of delegation - user to agent, agent to subagent, subagent to tool - in which the party harmed by an action, or asked to trust its result, is rarely the party that operated the agent. This document describes requirements and an evidence model for delegation and interaction traceability in such chains. The model is built on two mechanisms for which measured, independently verifiable evidence exists: (a) an append-only, hash-chained exhibit registry in which each admitted action is recorded exactly once and counters reconcile against registry contents, and (b) per-action attestation published at kernel level with measured publication latencies in the sub-microsecond-to-microsecond range. The document defines a traceability record, states what a verifier can and cannot conclude from a set of such records, and identifies the points at
which existing agent-protocol work - identity, authorisation, and transport - needs a common traceability layer. It defines no wire protocol of its own; it states the requirements a traceability mechanism must satisfy so that formats defined elsewhere can be evaluated against them.

section.name: Example
section.t: This example is one call from a context-map run of the reference agent (engine commit d6471f2) driven by a deterministic mock model, so it is a mock run in the sense of and would be refused at federation-tier admission (trace_run_kind_mock). It is reproduced as the implementation emitted it (JSON, with hexadecimal digests and nulls), trimmed to three of its nine segments. The call is the entropy judge, an ablated stage, reviewing a draft reply to an observer's request. The request is withheld and a stub sent in its place.

Reading it: the judge received the draft in full (a residual) and, in place of the request, a stub saying that an observer's request exists, open, of medium size and carrying no authority, that the draft quotes under 10% of it, and that its digest begins 3521ef40909a. The span [11, 236) of message 3 holds the stub line, whose own digest is sha256. sent_messages_match is true: the bus sent exactly these messages. The run predates the locale record of , so the segments carry no locale members.
